# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Pre-electoral polling plays an important role in understanding the public's political opinions and stances during election periods and can assist in predicting the outcomes of elections (Traugott, 2005). Polling on a state level is particularly insightful in the United States, as the results are determined by the Electoral College as opposed to national popular vote or preferential voting (Soumbatiants et al., 2006). Relative support for candidates on a state level can be estimated through polls, which can help assess how competitive each individual electoral contest is (Soumbatiants et al., 2006). While polling is an insightful tool, it does not always accurately reflect the final results of elections (Traugott, 2005). This is why it is important to understand what factors are associated with discrepancies between actual voting outcomes and polling estimates.

This analysis focuses on two polling features that may be associated with polling error: the proportion of undecided voters and the survey mode used to obtain responses. Only polls within 90 days of the elections will be considered. The number of undecided voters may increase uncertainty as to which party/candidate is more likely to win prior to the election. Similarly, certain survey modes may collect more accurate polling data than others. Through examining these variables, it may become evident that certain poll types will predict outcomes that are close to actual election results. Comparing 2012 and 2016 election polls and results allows the investigation of whether associations between polling error and polling characteristics are consistent across election periods. This analysis investigates how survey mode and reported undecided voter share are associated with state-level polling error, after accounting for time before Election Day, and whether these associations differ between the 2012 and 2016 elections.

# Method {#sec-method}

## Data

This study used three datasets: state-level presidential polling data from the 2012 and 2016 U.S. elections, obtained through the HuffPost Pollster/rOpenGov collection, and presidential election results from the MIT Election Data and Science Lab (MEDSL). The polling datasets contained 1,135 records from 2012 and 1,303 from 2016, including polling dates, states, survey modes, candidate support percentages, undecided voter share and sample sizes. Each polling record was treated as one observation. 

The election results were restricted to 2012 and 2016 and used to calculate actual state-level Democratic–Republican vote margins.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-descriptives
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of the variables used in the analysis."
data |>
  summarise(
    across(c(mpg, wt, hp),
           list(mean = mean, sd = sd),
           .names = "{.col}_{.fn}")
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(),
               names_to = c("Variable", ".value"),
               names_sep = "_") |>
  kable(digits = 2, col.names = c("Variable", "Mean", "SD"))
```

## Data Preparation and Sample Selection

The 2012 and 2016 polling datasets were combined after standardising state names, election years and polling dates to ensure consistency. Official election results were then matched to the polling data by state and year. Before calculating actual election margins, votes received by the same major-party candidate under different party labels were combined to avoid underestimating their total support. 

The analysis was restricted to polls ending within 90 days before Election Day. This period was selected to focus on polls conducted closer to the election, when voter preferences are more relevant to the final outcome. However, this restriction excludes earlier polls and limits the conclusions to the selected pre-election period. Records with invalid sample sizes, unavailable polling errors or missing undecided voter shares were excluded, leaving 1,561 complete observations. Missing undecided values were not replaced with zero because missing information does not necessarily indicate that no respondents were undecided. 

The primary analysis focused on Live Phone, Internet and IVR/Online polls, reducing the sample to 1,221 observations. These three survey modes were selected because they were represented in both election years, allowing more meaningful comparisons of their relationships with polling error. Other modes were excluded from the primary analysis due to limited or uneven coverage across years. Consequently, the findings cannot be generalised to all survey modes. 

Finally, two polls for which the sum of reported response percentages exceeded 102% were excluded from the main analysis, leaving 1,219 polls. As these totals do not necessarily indicate errors, both polls were included in a sensitivity analysis to assess whether their exclusion affected the results.

## Variable Construction

Polling accuracy was measured using the absolute difference between the reported Democratic–Republican polling margin and the actual election margin. 

The polling margin was calculated as: 

Poll Margin = Democratic % - Republican %

The actual election margin was calculated as: 

Actual Margin = ((Dvotes-Rvotes) / Total Votes) x 100

Votes received by the same candidate under different party labels were combined before calculating the actual margin.

Absolute polling error was then defined as: 

Absolute Error = Poll Margin - Actual Margin

Lower absolute error indicates greater polling accuracy. All margins and errors were expressed in percentage points. 

The main explanatory variables were reported undecided voter share and survey mode. Days before Election Day was calculated from each poll's end date, while election year distinguished the 2012 and 2016 observations. Undecided voter share was measured in percentage points, and survey mode and year were treated as categorical variables.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

<!-- See rubric: Discussion - connect to the question and context; examine limitations. -->

Interpret the result in relation to the research question and the wider context, then examine the limitations honestly. Keep claims within what the data support: these are observational 1974 model-year cars (`r n_obs` of them), so the association is not causal and may not generalise to modern vehicles.

## Limitations

The analysis performed identifies associations between predictors and response variables; this does not mean there is necessarily a causal relationship in the data. Other factors may also impact polling error. Polls with missing undecided voter shares were excluded, which may cause selection bias if such polls differ systematically from those that were included in the final dataset. In this investigation, only three survey modes were included; therefore, the associations found cannot be generalised to other survey modes. Polls from the same state and polling organisation could be related, which can affect the reliability of standard errors and confidence intervals, as the observations may not be independent. Finally, only two election periods were covered in this analysis, meaning that the findings may not be applicable to all elections, particularly historical elections that would not have used the same polling methods. It was also chosen to only analyse polls within a 90-day period of the election; it should be considered that associations may differ for polls outside of this period. The linear models created for this investigation are not highly accurate; other modelling methods could perform better. However, the focus of this investigation is linear modelling.

# Statistical appendix {#sec-appendix}

<!-- See rubric: Statistical appendix - fully reproducible, annotated analysis. -->

This appendix documents the analysis so the results above are fully reproducible. The annotated code reproduces the model and its assumption checks; the complete project (data, scripts, and commit history) is in the repository linked at the top.

## Statistical methods

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

# 1. Read the combined cleaned polling data and election results.

polls <- read_csv(
  "project datasets/clean/state_polls_combined_clean.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

elections <- read_csv(
  "project datasets/raw/1976-2024-president.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Check that each state-poll has a unique identifier.
sum(is.na(polls$poll_key)) # Count missing poll keys

sum(duplicated(polls$poll_key)) # Count duplicate poll keys

# 2. Count each major candidate's votes across all party label.

# This includes votes reported on extra ballot lines, especially in New York.
elections <- elections |>
  filter(year %in% c(2012, 2016)) |>
  mutate(
    state = str_replace_all(str_to_lower(state), " ", "-"),
    state = if_else(state == "district-of-columbia", "washington-dc", state),
    candidate_group = case_when(
      year == 2012 & candidate == "OBAMA, BARACK H." ~ "Democrat",
      year == 2012 & candidate == "ROMNEY, MITT" ~ "Republican",
      year == 2016 & candidate == "CLINTON, HILLARY" ~ "Democrat",
      year == 2016 & candidate == "TRUMP, DONALD J." ~ "Republican",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

# Check Democrat and Republican records with no candidate name
unknown_candidate <- elections |>
  filter(
    is.na(candidate),
    party_simplified %in% c("DEMOCRAT", "REPUBLICAN")
  ) |>
  select(year, state, party_simplified, candidatevotes)

print(unknown_candidate)

# Each state-year should have one total-votes value.
vote_totals <- elections |>
  group_by(year, state) |>
  summarise(total_votes = first(totalvotes),
            number_of_totals = n_distinct(totalvotes), .groups = "drop")

# Count state-year records with different total-vote values
print(sum(vote_totals$number_of_totals != 1))

# Count state-year records with missing total votes
print(sum(is.na(vote_totals$total_votes)))

# Count state-year records with zero or negative total votes
print(sum(vote_totals$total_votes <= 0, na.rm = TRUE))

candidate_votes <- elections |>
  filter(!is.na(candidate_group)) |>
  group_by(year, state, candidate_group) |>
  summarise(votes = sum(candidatevotes), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = candidate_group, values_from = votes)

actual_results <- candidate_votes |>
  left_join(vote_totals, by = c("year", "state")) |>
  mutate(actual_margin = 100 * (Democrat - Republican) / total_votes) |>
  select(year, state, actual_margin)

# Count duplicate state-year election results
print(sum(duplicated(actual_results[c("year", "state")])))

# Count missing actual margins
print(sum(is.na(actual_results$actual_margin)))

# 3. Join each poll to its state-year election result.
polls <- polls |>
  left_join(actual_results, by = c("year", "state")) |>
  mutate(
    poll_margin = case_when(
      year == 2012 ~ Obama - Romney,
      year == 2016 ~ Clinton - Trump
    ),
    absolute_error = abs(poll_margin - actual_margin)
  )

# Count polls without a matching election result
print(sum(is.na(polls$actual_margin)))

# 4. Flag polls whose reported response percentages add to more than 102%.
# Missing categories are ignored when adding reported values.
# A high total may reflect rounding or reporting differences, so we do not indicate that it is an error.
polls <- polls |>
  mutate(
    reported_total = case_when(
      year == 2012 ~ rowSums(across(c(Obama, Romney, Undecided, Other)), na.rm = TRUE),
      year == 2016 ~ rowSums(across(c(Clinton, Trump, Undecided, Other, Johnson, McMullin)), na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    unusual_total = reported_total > 102
  )

# 5. Select polls from the final 90 days.
# Exclude polls with missing or non-positive sample size.
# After data exploration, we agree to include 3 modes: Live Phone, Internet and IVR/Online polls into the model.
# Furthermore, we exclude the two flagged polls from the main sample
# and include them in a sensitivity check.

sample_90 <- polls |> filter(between(days_to_election, 0, 90))

valid <- sample_90 |>
  filter(!is.na(absolute_error), !is.na(sample_size), sample_size > 0)

# Polls that do not report undecided share are excluded; this may affect results.

complete <- valid |> filter(!is.na(Undecided))

selected <- complete |>
  filter(mode %in% c("Live Phone", "Internet", "IVR/Online")) |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(year, levels = c(2012, 2016)),
    mode = factor(mode, levels = c("Live Phone", "Internet", "IVR/Online"))
  )

main_data <- selected |> filter(!unusual_total)

sensitivity_data <- selected

unusual_records <- selected |>
  filter(unusual_total) |>
  select(poll_key, year, state, pollster, mode,
         Obama, Romney, Clinton, Trump, Undecided, Johnson, McMullin, Other,
         reported_total)

sample_counts <- tibble(
  stage = c("Cleaned polls", "Within 90 days", "Valid error and sample size",
            "Undecided reported", "Three modes", "Main sample"),
  remaining = c(nrow(polls), nrow(sample_90), nrow(valid), nrow(complete),
                nrow(selected), nrow(main_data))
) |>
  mutate(excluded_at_step = lag(remaining) - remaining)

print(sample_counts)

print(unusual_records, width = Inf)

print(table(main_data$year, main_data$mode))

# Save datasets
write_csv(main_data, "project datasets/analysis_data_final.csv")

write_csv(
  sensitivity_data,
  "project datasets/analysis_data_with_unusual.csv"
)

write_csv(sample_counts, "project datasets/sample_selection_counts.csv")

write_csv(unusual_records, "project datasets/unusual_records.csv")


```

## Sensitivity Check for Unusual Records {#sec-app-model}

```{r}
# Sensitivity check: compare estimates with and without the two flagged polls.
# Keep the other sample rules and model formula the same in both analyses.
# final model once it is agreed; use the same formula for both datasets.

model_formula <- absolute_error ~ year * (Undecided + days_to_election + mode)

model_main <- lm(model_formula, data = main_data)

model_with_unusual <- lm(model_formula, data = sensitivity_data)

# Check whether the two models have the same coefficient names
print(identical(
  names(coef(model_main)),
  names(coef(model_with_unusual))
))

# Count coefficients that could not be estimated
print(sum(is.na(coef(model_main))))

print(sum(is.na(coef(model_with_unusual))))

comparison <- tibble(
  term = names(coef(model_main)),
  main_estimate = unname(coef(model_main)),
  with_unusual_estimate = unname(coef(model_with_unusual))
) |>
  mutate(estimate_change = with_unusual_estimate - main_estimate)

print(summary(model_main))

print(summary(model_with_unusual))

print(comparison)

write_csv(comparison, "project datasets/sensitivity_comparison.csv")

# Polls may not be independent when they share a state or pollster. This may
# affect standard errors and p-values; discuss this limitation in the report.
# These observational results describe the selected polls and two elections;
# they do not establish causation or necessarily apply to future elections.

```

## Models

```{r}
# Read the main analysis dataset
analysis <- read_csv("project datasets/analysis_data_final.csv")

# Check the data
glimpse(analysis)
summary(analysis)

# Set reference groups: 2012 and Live Phone
analysis <- analysis |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(year, levels = c(2012, 2016)),
    mode = factor(
      mode,
      levels = c("Live Phone", "Internet", "IVR/Online")
    )
  )

table(analysis$year, analysis$mode)

# Model 1: additive model
model_add <- lm(
  absolute_error ~ Undecided + days_to_election + mode + year,
  data = analysis
)

# Model 2: associations can differ by year
model_interaction <- lm(
  absolute_error ~ year * (Undecided + days_to_election + mode),
  data = analysis
)
```

## Model comparison

```{r}
# See the estimated coefficients

summary(model_add)
summary(model_interaction)

# Compare the two nested models
anova(model_add, model_interaction)

# Check diagnostic plots for the interaction model
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model_interaction)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Try a model with a transformed response
model_log <- lm(
  log1p(absolute_error) ~
    year * (Undecided + days_to_election + mode),
  data = analysis
)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model_log)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

summary(model_log)

# Check the largest Cook's distances
head(sort(cooks.distance(model_log), decreasing = TRUE), 10)
```

```{r}

# Inspect the three largest Cook's distances for the log model
analysis[c(96, 219, 299),
         c("state", "year", "pollster", "mode", "absolute_error")]

model_log_additive <- lm(
  log1p(absolute_error) ~ Undecided + days_to_election + mode + year,
  data = analysis
)

anova(model_log_additive, model_log)

# Fit the same model using a square-root transformation (Final model)
model_sqrt <- lm(
  sqrt(absolute_error) ~ year * (Undecided + days_to_election + mode),
  data = analysis
)

# Check diagnostics
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model_sqrt)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

summary(model_sqrt)

head(sort(cooks.distance(model_sqrt), decreasing = TRUE), 5)

# Inspect the five largest Cook's distances for the square-root model
analysis[c(96, 7, 299, 219, 237),
         c("state", "year", "pollster", "mode", "absolute_error")]

model_sqrt_additive <- lm(
  sqrt(absolute_error) ~ Undecided + days_to_election + mode + year,
  data = analysis
)

anova(model_sqrt_additive, model_sqrt)
```

@tbl-model-detail reports the full fitted model with 95% confidence intervals.

## Assumption checks {#sec-app-checks}

@fig-diagnostics shows the residual diagnostics used to check the linear-model assumptions of constant variance and approximately normal residuals.

```{r}
#| label: fig-diagnostics
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics: residuals vs fitted values (left) and a normal Q-Q plot (right)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(model, which = 1)   # residuals vs fitted: linearity and equal variance
plot(model, which = 2)   # normal Q-Q: normality of residuals
```
